mainTopic: Owners "with" the borrower, מה לי לשקר and witnesses, a plain 'put it down,' and a lender holding collateral
overview: This amud opens by finishing two stories in which רב פפא and then רבא rule that someone must pay. Each time the רבנן object that the owner was "with" the person holding the item (בבעלים). Each time new facts show the ruling was right: the owner was drinking beer, and the sheet was taken without permission. Next, a renter takes a road the owner forbade, and the donkey dies. רבא would believe the renter's claim that there was no water there, using מה לי לשקר. אביי answers that this reasoning does not work when witnesses can check the facts. The גמרא then asks whether saying just 'put it down' makes someone a שומר חנם. It tries to answer from the משנה and from a dispute between תנאים, but neither source settles the question. Finally, the גמרא asks whether the משנה's rule, that a lender holding collateral is a שומר שכר, goes against רבי אליעזר. It answers by splitting the cases by when the collateral was taken, and a new challenge to that answer begins at the end of the amud.

steps.title: The cloak is stolen and רב פפא rules the guardians must pay
steps.stepSummary: The story of the cloak, which began just before this, ends with the cloak being stolen. רב פפא rules that the ones holding it must pay.
steps.simpleTranslation: Before he came back, it was stolen. They came before רב פפא, and he ruled that they had to pay.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא finishes a story about a cloak that was stolen. רב פפא rules that the people holding it must pay for it.
steps.deeperAnalysis: These people were guarding the cloak, and a guardian who is responsible for theft normally pays when the item is stolen. So רב פפא's ruling looks like the normal rule. The next step questions whether this case is an exception.

keyTerms.meaning: he ruled them liable (they must pay)
an אמורא, the judge in this story

phrases.english: Before he came back, it was stolen.
They came before Rav Pappa,
he ruled them liable.

steps.triggerLanguage: אֲתוֹ לְקַמֵּיהּ דְּרַב פָּפָּא חַיְּיבִינְהוּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Finishes a story that began just before this part of the daf.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: רב פפא rules that the ones holding the cloak must pay for the stolen cloak.

steps.title: The רבנן object: the owner was with them
steps.stepSummary: The רבנן challenge רב פפא. The owner was helping at the time, so this is שמירה בבעלים, and in that case there is no payment.
steps.simpleTranslation: The רבנן said to רב פפא: This is a case of guarding while the owner is with them! He was embarrassed.
steps.whatsHappening: The רבנן attack רב פפא's ruling. They say this case should be exempt because the owner was "with" the guardians, and רב פפא is embarrassed.
steps.deeperAnalysis: There is a rule that if the owner is working for the borrower or guard at the time, the borrower or guard does not pay (בבעלים). The רבנן assumed the cloak's owner was busy helping the others, so they thought רב פפא's ruling ignored this exemption.

keyTerms.meaning: guarding while the owner is working with or for the guard, which brings an exemption

steps.confusionAlert: "בבעלים" does not just mean the owner is standing nearby. It means the owner is working for, or helping, the borrower or guard at that time.

phrases.english: The Rabbis said to Rav Pappa:
This is guarding with the owners!
phrases.notes: They assumed the cloak's owner was working for the guardians at that moment, so no payment should be owed.

phrases.english: He was embarrassed.

steps.triggerLanguage: אֲמַרוּ לֵיהּ רַבָּנַן לְרַב פָּפָּא הָא שְׁמִירָה בִּבְעָלִים הִיא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the ruling of step 1.
steps.kashyaTarget: רב פפא's ruling that they must pay
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: When the owner is helping at the time, the guards are exempt. Since the owner was helping here, the ruling seems wrong.

steps.title: The truth comes out: the owner was drinking beer
steps.stepSummary: It later turned out the owner was drinking beer at that moment, not helping. So the exemption never applied, and רב פפא was right.
steps.simpleTranslation: In the end, it came out that at that time he was drinking beer.
steps.whatsHappening: New facts come out that defend רב פפא. The owner was not helping at that moment, so the case was never שמירה בבעלים.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The exemption needs the owner to be actually working for the guard at the time. Because he was drinking beer and not helping, the normal rule applies and they must pay.

keyTerms.meaning: the matter was revealed, it came out

phrases.english: In the end, the matter was revealed
that at that time he was drinking beer.

steps.whatToRemember: The בבעלים exemption works only if the owner is truly working for the borrower or guard at that moment.
steps.triggerLanguage: לְסוֹף אִיגַּלַּאי מִילְּתָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the objection of step 2 by correcting the facts.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The owner was helping, so the exemption applies.
steps.terutzMaskana: The owner was drinking beer, so there was no exemption, and the payment ruling stands.

steps.title: The tall man, the short man, and the washed-away sheet
steps.stepSummary: A new story. A short man crossing a river puts his cloak on the tall man's donkey and wraps himself in the tall man's sheet. The water washes the sheet away.
steps.simpleTranslation: Two people were traveling, one tall and one short. The tall one rode a donkey and had a sheet. The short one wore a cloak and walked. At a river, the short one put his cloak on the donkey, took the tall one's sheet, and covered himself with it. The water swept the sheet away.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא begins a new story that sets up the next ruling. The tall man's sheet is lost while the short man is using it.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The details matter for the ruling. The short man's cloak is resting on the tall man's donkey at the same moment the short man is using the tall man's sheet. That sets up the question of whether the tall man was "with" him.

phrases.english: There were these two people
who were walking on the road,
one tall and one short.
The tall one was riding a donkey
and he had a sheet,
the short one was covered with a cloak
and was walking on his feet.
When they reached a river,
he took his cloak and placed it on the donkey,
phrases.notes: "He" is the short man, keeping his cloak dry.

phrases.english: and he took the sheet of that one and covered himself with it.
The water swept away his sheet.

steps.triggerLanguage: הָנְהוּ בֵּי תְרֵי דַּהֲווֹ קָא מְסַגּוּ בְּאוֹרְחָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: A new story on the same theme: the owner being "with" the borrower.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Sets up the facts: the sheet was lost while the short man was using it.

steps.title: רבא rules that the short man must pay
steps.stepSummary: The case comes to רבא, who rules that the short man must pay for the sheet.
steps.simpleTranslation: He came before רבא, and רבא ruled him liable.
steps.whatsHappening: רבא gives his ruling: the short man pays for the lost sheet. The next step will challenge this.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A borrower normally pays even for accidents, so this looks like the standard rule. The question is whether the tall man's donkey carrying the short man's cloak makes this an exempt case.

keyTerms.meaning: an אמורא, the judge in this story

phrases.english: He came before Rava,
he ruled him liable.

steps.triggerLanguage: אֲתָא לְקַמֵּיהּ דְּרָבָא חַיְּיבֵיהּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives the ruling for the story in step 4.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The short man must pay for the sheet.

steps.title: The רבנן object: it is borrowing with the owner
steps.stepSummary: The רבנן ask why he should pay, since this is שאלה בבעלים: the tall man's donkey was serving the short man by carrying his cloak.
steps.simpleTranslation: The רבנן said to רבא: Why? This is borrowing with the owner! He was embarrassed.
steps.whatsHappening: The רבנן challenge רבא's ruling, and רבא is embarrassed. The story has the same shape as the רב פפא story.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The רבנן see the tall man as helping the short man at the very moment of the borrowing, since the short man's cloak was riding on his donkey. A borrower whose owner is helping him at that time is exempt.

keyTerms.meaning: borrowing while the owner is working with or for the borrower, which brings an exemption

phrases.english: The Rabbis said to Rava: Why?
This is borrowing with the owners!
He was embarrassed.

steps.triggerLanguage: אֲמַרוּ לֵיהּ רַבָּנַן לְרָבָא אַמַּאי שְׁאֵלָה בִּבְעָלִים הִיא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges רבא's ruling in step 5.
steps.kashyaTarget: רבא's ruling that the short man must pay
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The owner was serving the borrower at the time of the borrowing, so the exemption should apply.

steps.title: The truth comes out: he took the sheet without permission
steps.stepSummary: It turned out the short man took the sheet, and put his cloak on the donkey, without the tall man knowing. So this was not borrowing at all, and רבא was right.
steps.simpleTranslation: In the end it came out that he took it without the owner knowing, and he placed it without the owner knowing.
steps.whatsHappening: New facts defend רבא's ruling. The short man acted without the tall man's knowledge, so this was taking, not borrowing.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The exemption only works for a real borrowing. Taking something without the owner knowing makes a person like a thief, and a thief pays for accidents. The owner also didn't knowingly carry the cloak, so he wasn't "helping" either.

phrases.english: In the end, the matter was revealed
that without his knowledge he took it,
phrases.notes: The short man took the tall man's sheet without asking.

phrases.english: and without his knowledge he placed it.
phrases.notes: This is the cloak he put on the donkey; the tall man never agreed to carry it.

steps.whatToRemember: Both stories teach the same thing: the בבעלים exemption needs a real borrowing or guarding, and the owner must truly be helping at that moment.
steps.triggerLanguage: לְסוֹף אִיגַּלַּאי מִילְּתָא דִּבְלָא דַּעְתֵּיהּ שַׁקְלֵיהּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the objection of step 6 by correcting the facts.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: This was a borrowing while the owner was serving him, so he is exempt.
steps.terutzMaskana: It was taken and placed without permission, so it was not a borrowing and he must pay.

steps.title: A renter takes the forbidden road and the donkey dies
steps.stepSummary: An owner rents out his donkey and warns against the road of נהר פקוד because of water. The renter goes that way anyway, and the donkey dies.
steps.simpleTranslation: A man rented a donkey to someone and said: Look, don't go by the road of נהר פקוד where there is water. Go by the road of נרש where there is no water. He went by the road of נהר פקוד, and the donkey died.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא begins a third story, about a renter who broke the owner's condition. It sets up a question that will be decided next.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The owner made a clear condition because of a specific danger, water. The renter broke the condition, and the donkey died. Whether he must pay depends on what comes next.

keyTerms.meaning: a place name; its road had water
a place name; its road had no water

phrases.aramaic: הָהוּא גַּבְרָא דְּאוֹגַר לֵיהּ חֲמָרָא לְחַבְרֵיהּ,
phrases.english: A certain man rented a donkey to his fellow,
he said to him: Look,
do not go by the road of Nehar Pekod
where there is water,
go by the road of Neresh
where there is no water.
He went by the road of Nehar Pekod
and the donkey died.

steps.triggerLanguage: הָהוּא גַּבְרָא דְּאוֹגַר לֵיהּ חֲמָרָא לְחַבְרֵיהּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: A new story about a renter who broke the owner's condition.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Sets up the facts: the forbidden road was taken and the donkey died.

steps.title: The renter's claim: I went that way, but there was no water
steps.stepSummary: The renter admits he took the forbidden road but claims there was no water there, so the road was not what killed the donkey.
steps.simpleTranslation: When he came back, he said: Yes, I went by the road of נהר פקוד, but there was no water.
steps.whatsHappening: The renter gives his defense. The גמרא is setting up the ruling on his claim, which comes after this.
steps.deeperAnalysis: He admits breaking the condition but argues that the danger the owner feared, water, wasn't there. So in his view the death had nothing to do with his change of route. Whether this claim helps him is the question the גמרא will deal with next.

phrases.english: When he came, he said:
Yes, I went by the road of Nehar Pekod,
but there was no water.
phrases.notes: He means the donkey died from something else, not from the water the owner was afraid of.

steps.triggerLanguage: כִּי אֲתָא אָמַר אִין בְּאוֹרְחָא דִּנְהַר פְּקוֹד אֲזַלִי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives the renter's defense in the story from step 8.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The renter claims his change of route did not cause the death, because the forbidden road had no water.

steps.title: רבא believes the renter because he could have told a better lie
steps.stepSummary: רבא accepts the renter's claim that there was no water, using the reasoning of מה לי לשקר.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבא said: Why would he lie? If he wanted to lie, he could have said, 'I went on the road of נרש.'
steps.whatsHappening: רבא rules on the donkey case and sides with the renter. The renter admitted something that hurts him, so he is probably telling the truth.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The renter openly admitted he took the forbidden road, which is a claim that hurts him. If he were a liar, he could simply have said he took the allowed road. רבא reasons that a person who passes up an easier lie should be believed about the part that helps him, namely that there was no water.

keyTerms.meaning: 'Why would I lie?' He could have made a better false claim, so we believe the claim he actually made.
The road of נרש, the route the owner allowed

phrases.english: Rava said to him:
Why would he lie?
If he wanted, he could have said to him:
I went on the road of Neresh.
phrases.notes: Neresh was the safe road the owner allowed, so this would have been an easy lie that cleared him completely.

steps.triggerLanguage: אֲמַר לֵיהּ רָבָא: מָה לֵיהּ לְשַׁקֵּר
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives a ruling on the renter's claim from step 9.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The renter is believed that there was no water, because he could have claimed he took the permitted road.

steps.title: אביי: this reasoning does not work when witnesses can check
steps.stepSummary: אביי rejects רבא's reasoning because the facts can be checked by witnesses.
steps.simpleTranslation: אביי said to him: We do not say 'Why would I lie?' in a place where there are witnesses.
steps.whatsHappening: אביי pushes back on רבא. He says מה לי לשקר cannot help the renter here.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Whether there was water on the road of נהר פקוד is something witnesses can come and testify about. When the truth can be checked, the fact that a person could have told a different lie proves nothing. The renter therefore cannot win just by relying on מה לי לשקר.

keyTerms.meaning: In a place where there are witnesses who can establish the facts
We do not say (apply) this reasoning

steps.whatToRemember: מה לי לשקר does not work בִּמְקוֹם עֵדִים, where the facts can be established by witnesses.
steps.whyThisMatters: This is a basic limit on the rule of מה לי לשקר that appears throughout ש״ס.

phrases.english: Abaye said to him:
'Why would I lie,' in a place where there are witnesses,
we do not say.

steps.triggerLanguage: אֲמַר לֵיהּ אַבָּיֵי: מָה לִי לְשַׁקֵּר בִּמְקוֹם עֵדִים לָא אָמְרִינַן
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Rejects רבא's reasoning from step 10.
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: The use of מה לי לשקר in this case
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: The facts can be checked by witnesses, so the 'better lie' argument has no force.

steps.title: 'Put it before me' versus 'put it before yourself'
steps.stepSummary: The משנה says 'put it before me' makes a שומר חנם. רב הונא adds that 'put it before yourself' makes him no שומר at all.
steps.simpleTranslation: If one says, 'Watch this for me,' and the other answers, 'Put it before me,' he is an unpaid watchman. רב הונא said: If he answered, 'Put it before yourself,' he is neither an unpaid watchman nor a paid watchman.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא moves to a new topic, the משנה's rule about watching items. רב הונא adds a case where the person takes on no responsibility.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Saying 'before me' shows the person is accepting the item into his care, so he becomes a שומר חנם. Saying 'before yourself' signals that the owner should keep watching it himself. That person accepts no duty at all.

keyTerms.meaning: An unpaid watchman, who is responsible only for negligence
A paid watchman, who has more responsibility

steps.confusionAlert: Watch the two similar words: לְפָנַי (before me) makes him a שומר, while לְפָנֶיךָ (before you) makes him not a שומר at all.

phrases.english: 'Watch for me,' and he said to him, 'Put it before me':
he is an unpaid watchman.
Rav Huna said:
If he said to him, 'Put it before yourself,'

phrases.aramaic: אֵינוֹ לֹא שׁוֹמֵר חִנָּם וְלֹא שׁוֹמֵר שָׂכָר.
phrases.english: he is neither an unpaid watchman nor a paid watchman.

steps.triggerLanguage: שְׁמוֹר לִי וְאָמַר לוֹ הַנַּח לְפָנַי שׁוֹמֵר חִנָּם. אָמַר רַב הוּנָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts a new topic from the משנה, separate from the donkey case.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: 'Before me' makes a שומר חנם. 'Before yourself' creates no watching duty.

steps.title: What if he just says 'put it down'?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks what the law is when the person says only 'put it down,' without 'before me' or 'before yourself.'
steps.simpleTranslation: A question was asked: If he said just 'put it down,' what is the law?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא raises a question about the in-between case. This sets up the attempts to answer it in the next steps.
steps.deeperAnalysis: 'Before me' means he accepts responsibility, and 'before yourself' means he does not. A plain 'put it down' could go either way, so it is unclear whether he becomes a שומר חנם.

keyTerms.meaning: A question was asked among the scholars

phrases.english: It was asked of them:
'Put it down,' without specifying, what is the law?

steps.triggerLanguage: אִיבַּעְיָא לְהוּ: הַנַּח סְתָמָא, מַאי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Asks about the case between the two cases in step 12.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Whether a plain 'put it down' makes the person a שומר חנם.

steps.title: A proof from the משנה that a plain 'put it down' means nothing
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא infers from the משנה's wording 'before me' that a plain 'put it down' creates no responsibility.
steps.simpleTranslation: Come and hear: 'Watch for me,' and he said 'Put it before me,' he is an unpaid watchman. This implies that a plain statement is nothing.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא tries to answer the question from the exact words of the משנה.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The משנה needed to say 'before me' to make him a שומר חנם. That suggests that without 'before me,' he would not be a שומר at all.

keyTerms.meaning: Come and hear, which introduces a proof
And it is nothing, meaning no responsibility

phrases.english: Come and hear:

phrases.aramaic: שְׁמוֹר לִי וְאָמַר לוֹ הַנַּח לְפָנַי –
phrases.english: 'Watch for me,' and he said to him, 'Put it before me':
he is an unpaid watchman.
So a plain statement is nothing.

steps.triggerLanguage: תָּא שְׁמַע: שְׁמוֹר לִי וְאָמַר לוֹ הַנַּח לְפָנַי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Tries to answer the question of step 13.
steps.raayaObject: A plain 'put it down' creates no watching duty.

steps.title: On the contrary: רב הונא's wording points the other way
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא answers that רב הונא's wording suggests the opposite: a plain 'put it down' does make him a שומר חנם.
steps.simpleTranslation: On the contrary! Since רב הונא said 'Put it before yourself,' only then is he neither an unpaid nor a paid watchman. This implies that with a plain statement he is an unpaid watchman!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא pushes back on the proof by drawing the opposite inference from רב הונא's words.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רב הונא needed the words 'before yourself' to free the person from all duty. That suggests that a plain 'put it down' would still make him a שומר חנם. So one inference cancels out the other.

phrases.english: On the contrary,
since Rav Huna said, 'Put it before yourself,'

phrases.aramaic: הוּא דְּאֵינוֹ לֹא שׁוֹמֵר חִנָּם וְלֹא שׁוֹמֵר שָׂכָר,
phrases.english: only then is he neither an unpaid watchman nor a paid watchman,
so with a plain statement he is an unpaid watchman!

steps.triggerLanguage: אַדְּרַבָּה, מִדְּאָמַר רַב הוּנָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Rejects the proof of step 14 by showing an opposite inference.
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: The inference drawn from the משנה
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: An equally strong inference from רב הונא's wording points the opposite way.

steps.title: Nothing can be learned from here
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא concludes that the question cannot be settled from these sources.
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather, nothing can be learned from this.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא gives up on this attempted proof. The question about a plain 'put it down' stays open for now.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The two inferences contradict each other, so neither one proves anything. The question remains unanswered.

keyTerms.meaning: There is nothing to learn from it

phrases.english: Rather, from this there is nothing to learn.

steps.triggerLanguage: אֶלָּא מֵהָא לֵיכָּא לְמִשְׁמַע מִינַּהּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Closes the proof attempt of steps 14–15.
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: Neither the משנה nor רב הונא settles the case of a plain 'put it down.'

steps.title: Maybe this question is a dispute between תנאים
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא suggests that the question of a plain 'put it down' matches a dispute between the תנא קמא and רבי about items brought into a courtyard with permission.
steps.simpleTranslation: Shall we say it is like a dispute between תנאים? If he brought it in with the permission of the courtyard owner, the owner is liable. רבי says: In all cases he is not liable until the owner accepts upon himself to watch.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא proposes that this question was already argued by תנאים. This sets up a discussion of whether that comparison holds.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In the case in בבא קמא, the owner only gave permission and did not promise to watch, which is like a plain 'put it down.' The תנא קמא holds him liable, so for him permission alone creates responsibility. רבי requires a clear acceptance to watch, so for him a plain 'put it down' would mean nothing.

keyTerms.meaning: Shall we say this is a dispute between תנאים?
That he accepts upon himself to watch

phrases.english: Shall we say it is like a dispute of Tannaim?

phrases.aramaic: אִם הִכְנִיס בִּרְשׁוּת בַּעַל חָצֵר – חַיָּיב.
phrases.english: If he brought it in with the permission of the courtyard owner, he is liable.
phrases.notes: This is a משנה in בבא קמא 47b. 'He is liable' refers to the courtyard owner, if the items get damaged.

phrases.english: Rabbi says:
In all of them he is not liable

phrases.aramaic: עַד שֶׁיְּקַבֵּל עָלָיו בַּעַל הַבַּיִת לִשְׁמוֹר.
phrases.english: until the owner accepts upon himself to watch.

steps.triggerLanguage: לֵימָא כְּתַנָּאֵי: אִם הִכְנִיס בִּרְשׁוּת בַּעַל חָצֵר חַיָּיב
steps.relationToPreviousStep: After the failed proof in steps 14–16, tries a new source for the question of step 13.
steps.raayaObject: The question of a plain 'put it down' depends on a dispute between תנאים.
steps.raayaSupportSource: The משנה in בבא קמא 47b: the תנא קמא against רבי

steps.title: The Rabbis' courtyard ruling may not apply to a market
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא rejects the comparison from step 17. The רבנן may have held the courtyard owner responsible only because a courtyard is a place that can be guarded. A market cannot be guarded.
steps.simpleTranslation: How do you know the cases match? Maybe the רבנן ruled that way only about a courtyard, which can be guarded. When the owner said 'bring it in,' he meant 'bring it in so I can guard it for you.' But a market cannot be guarded, so 'put it down' there means 'put it down and sit and guard it yourself.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא pushes back on step 17. Even the רבנן, who make the courtyard owner a שומר, might agree that a plain 'put it down' in a market creates no responsibility.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A courtyard is a guarded space, so letting someone bring items in sounds like an offer to watch them. A market is open to everyone, so 'put it down' there sounds like 'watch it yourself.' The two cases are different, so the dispute does not settle our question.

keyTerms.meaning: From where do you know? (a challenge to an assumption)
A place that can be guarded

phrases.english: From where do you know this?
phrases.notes: He means: how do you know the courtyard dispute really matches our case of 'put it down'?

phrases.aramaic: דִּלְמָא עַד כָּאן לָא קָאָמְרִי רַבָּנַן הָתָם
phrases.english: Perhaps the Rabbis only say their ruling there
phrases.notes: The רבנן are the ones in step 17 who make the courtyard owner responsible.

phrases.english: in a courtyard, which is a place that can be guarded,
and when he said to him 'bring it in,'
he was saying to him, 'bring it in so I will guard it for you.'

phrases.aramaic: אֲבָל הָכָא, שׁוּקָא לָאו בַּר נַטּוֹרֵי הוּא,
phrases.english: But here, a market is not a place that can be guarded,
so he was saying to him, 'put it down, and sit and guard it yourself.'

steps.triggerLanguage: מִמַּאי? דִּלְמָא עַד כָּאן לָא קָאָמְרִי רַבָּנַן הָתָם
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Rejects the comparison proposed in step 17
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: The claim that the רבנן's courtyard ruling means a plain 'put it down' creates responsibility
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: A courtyard can be guarded and a market cannot, so the words carry different meanings in each place

steps.title: רבי's courtyard ruling may not apply to a market either
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא shows the opposite side also fails. רבי may have freed the courtyard owner only because entering a private courtyard needs permission. In a market, asking permission makes sense only if he means 'I will guard it.'
steps.simpleTranslation: Or else: maybe רבי ruled that way only about a person's own courtyard. There the visitor needs permission to bring things in, so permission only means 'sit and guard it yourself.' But here in the market he was saying 'put it down and I will guard it.' If you think he meant 'put it down and guard it yourself,' why would the owner need permission to put something down in a public place?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא gives a second rejection, from the other direction. Even רבי, who frees the courtyard owner, might agree that a plain 'put it down' in a market does create responsibility.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In a private courtyard, 'yes' can simply mean 'you may come in,' with no promise to guard. In a public market no one needs permission to set something down. So if the owner asked and the other man answered 'put it down,' it must mean 'I will watch it.' Since neither side of the dispute decides our question, the comparison falls away.
steps.whatToRemember: The question of a plain 'put it down' does not depend on the courtyard dispute. Each side's reasoning could change in a market, so the question stays open.

phrases.aramaic: אִי נָמֵי: עַד כָּאן לָא קָאָמַר רַבִּי הָתָם
phrases.english: Alternatively: perhaps Rebbi only says his ruling there
about his own courtyard,

phrases.aramaic: דִּלְעַיּוֹלֵי רְשׁוּתָא קָא בָעֵי לְמִשְׁקַל מִינֵּיהּ
phrases.english: since to bring things in he needs to take permission from him,
and when he gives him permission to bring them in,
he was saying to him, 'sit and guard it yourself.'

phrases.aramaic: אֲבָל הָכָא – ״הַנַּח וַאֲנָא מְנַטַּרְנָא״ קָאָמַר לֵיהּ.
phrases.english: But here, he was saying to him, 'put it down and I will guard it.'
For if you would think
that he was saying to him, 'put it down, and sit and guard it yourself,'

phrases.aramaic: אִי לְאוֹתֹבֵה, רְשׁוּתָא בָּעֵי לְמִשְׁקַל מִינֵּיהּ?
phrases.english: would he need to take permission from him just to set it down?

steps.triggerLanguage: אִי נָמֵי: עַד כָּאן לָא קָאָמַר רַבִּי הָתָם
steps.relationToPreviousStep: A second rejection of step 17, from the opposite side
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: The claim that רבי's courtyard ruling means a plain 'put it down' creates no responsibility
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: In a courtyard permission is needed just to enter. In a market no permission is needed, so the request must have been about guarding.

steps.title: The משנה: a lender holding collateral is a paid guardian
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא turns to the next ruling in the משנה. Someone who lent money and holds collateral is a שומר שכר over it.
steps.simpleTranslation: If he lent him money on collateral, he is a paid guardian.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא opens a new topic by quoting a line from the משנה. It is setting up a question about that line.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The lender gets no fee for guarding the collateral, yet the משנה treats him as a שומר שכר, who is responsible even for theft and loss. The next step will ask whether every תנא agrees with this.

keyTerms.meaning: Collateral; an item given as security for a loan
Paid guardian, responsible even for theft and loss

phrases.english: If he lent him money on collateral, he is a paid guardian.

steps.triggerLanguage: הִלְוָהוּ עַל הַמַּשְׁכּוֹן – שׁוֹמֵר שָׂכָר
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts a new topic from the משנה
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A lender holding collateral has the status of a שומר שכר

steps.title: Does the משנה go against רבי אליעזר?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא suggests the משנה disagrees with רבי אליעזר. He rules that if the collateral is lost, the lender swears and still collects his loan.
steps.simpleTranslation: Shall we say our משנה does not follow רבי אליעזר? For a ברייתא teaches: if someone lends to his friend on collateral and the collateral is lost, the lender swears and takes his money. These are the words of רבי אליעזר.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks whether the משנה's ruling clashes with רבי אליעזר. It brings a ברייתא to show his view.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A שומר שכר must pay for an item that gets lost. רבי אליעזר instead lets the lender swear that he was not careless and still collect the full loan. That sounds like the lender is not a שומר שכר, which seems to contradict the משנה.

keyTerms.meaning: Shall we say? (opens a suggestion the גמרא will test)

phrases.english: Shall we say our משנה does not follow רבי אליעזר?
For it is taught in a ברייתא:
One who lends to his friend on collateral
and the collateral was lost:
he swears and takes his money,
phrases.notes: The lender swears that he was not careless, and then the borrower still has to repay the loan.

phrases.english: these are the words of רבי אליעזר.

steps.triggerLanguage: לֵימָא מַתְנִיתִין דְּלָא כְּרַבִּי אֱלִיעֶזֶר
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges whether the משנה just quoted fits רבי אליעזר's view
steps.kashyaTarget: The משנה's ruling that a lender holding collateral is a שומר שכר
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: רבי אליעזר lets the lender swear and collect after a loss, which treats him like a שומר חנם rather than a שומר שכר

steps.title: רבי עקיבא: if the collateral is lost, the loan is lost
steps.stepSummary: The ברייתא continues with רבי עקיבא's view. The borrower can say 'you lent only on the collateral,' so once it is lost the debt is gone. Where there is also a loan document, everyone agrees the loan is lost with the collateral.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי עקיבא says: the borrower can say to him, 'Didn't you lend to me only on the collateral? The collateral is lost, so your money is lost.' But if he lent him a thousand זוז with a loan document and the borrower left him collateral for it, everyone agrees: if the collateral is lost, his money is lost.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא finishes quoting the ברייתא. It gives רבי עקיבא's opposing view and a case where everyone agrees.
steps.deeperAnalysis: For רבי עקיבא, the collateral stands in place of the loan, so losing it wipes out the debt. When there is a loan document, the collateral is not needed as proof of the loan. So everyone agrees it was given as security, and its loss cancels the debt.

keyTerms.meaning: Was it anything but...? (a rhetorical 'didn't you only...')

steps.confusionAlert: Do not mix up the two cases. רבי אליעזר and רבי עקיבא argue only when there is collateral without a loan document. With a document, both agree the loan is lost along with the collateral.

phrases.aramaic: רַבִּי עֲקִיבָא אוֹמֵר: יָכוֹל לוֹמַר לוֹ:
phrases.english: רבי עקיבא says: the borrower can say to him:
'Didn't you lend to me only on the collateral?'
'The collateral is lost, so your money is lost.'
But if he lent him a thousand זוז with a loan document
and the borrower left him collateral for them,
everyone agrees:
if the collateral is lost, his money is lost.

steps.triggerLanguage: רַבִּי עֲקִיבָא אוֹמֵר: יָכוֹל לוֹמַר לוֹ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues the ברייתא quoted in step 21
steps.mimraCoreRuling: According to רבי עקיבא, lost collateral cancels the loan. Where there is a loan document, everyone agrees it does.

steps.title: Different timing of the collateral solves the contradiction
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא says the משנה can follow רבי אליעזר after all. One source deals with collateral taken at the time of the loan, and the other with collateral taken later.
steps.simpleTranslation: You can even say the משנה follows רבי אליעזר, and there is no difficulty. Here it is a case where he took the collateral when he gave the loan. There it is a case where he took the collateral not at the time of the loan.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the problem from step 21. It shows that the משנה and רבי אליעזר are not really arguing, because they are talking about two different cases.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The split depends on when the lender took the collateral. When he took it at the time of the loan, it mainly served as proof that a loan happened, so רבי אליעזר lets him swear and still collect. When he took it later, it was clearly meant to secure payment, so the משנה treats him as a שומר שכר.

keyTerms.meaning: Even if you say: a way of keeping a view that seemed to be ruled out
And it is not difficult: the contradiction is about to be solved
Here... there: splitting two sources into two different cases
At the time of his loan, when the money was first lent

steps.whyThisMatters: This shows that the timing of the collateral can change the lender's legal position over it.

phrases.english: Even if you say it follows רבי אליעזר,
phrases.notes: He means our משנה, which calls the lender a שומר שכר, can still match רבי אליעזר.

phrases.english: it is not difficult:
here, it is where he took his collateral at the time of his loan,
phrases.notes: This is the ברייתא with רבי אליעזר's ruling, where the lender swears and still collects.

phrases.english: there, it is where he took his collateral not at the time of his loan.
phrases.notes: This is our משנה, where the lender is a שומר שכר.

steps.triggerLanguage: אֲפִילּוּ תֵּימָא רַבִּי אֱלִיעֶזֶר, וְלָא קַשְׁיָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge from step 21 that the משנה disagrees with רבי אליעזר.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Splitting the cases (כָּאן... כָּאן) by when the collateral was taken
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The משנה seemed to argue with רבי אליעזר, who lets the lender collect even after the collateral is lost.
steps.terutzMaskana: Both can be true. Collateral taken at the time of the loan follows רבי אליעזר's ruling. Collateral taken later makes the lender a שומר שכר, as in the משנה.

steps.title: A new challenge begins against the timing split
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא starts to push back on the answer from step 23 by suggesting both sources describe the same kind of case. The sentence continues in the next part of the text.
steps.simpleTranslation: But don't both this one and that one...
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא is setting up a new challenge to the answer it just gave. Only the opening words appear here, and the rest of the question comes next.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The words 'this and that' point to the משנה and the ברייתא. The גמרא is about to claim they really describe the same situation. If so, the timing split from step 23 would fall apart.

keyTerms.meaning: But isn't it so: opens a challenge
This and that: both sources together

steps.confusionAlert: This sentence is not finished on this amud. The rest of the question, about what both sources describe, is on the next amud.

phrases.english: But don't both this and that,
phrases.notes: 'This and that' means the משנה and the ברייתא. The question continues in the next line of the daf.

steps.triggerLanguage: וְהָא אִידֵּי וְאִידֵּי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts to challenge the case split given in step 23.
steps.kashyaTarget: The answer in step 23 that splits the משנה and the ברייתא by when the collateral was taken.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: It is about to argue that both sources describe the same kind of case, so the split cannot explain the difference.
